title: MS Excel
summary: Spreadsheet structure, cell references, functions, formula errors, charts and shortcuts. Excel gives the most 'compute-the-answer' questions in CKT - COUNT/IF/VLOOKP outputs are verifiable, so marks are safe.

subtopics.title: Workbook, cells and references
subtopics.concept: **MS Excel** is a spreadsheet program. Its work area is a grid of **rows** and **columns**. Where a row and a column meet is a **cell**, named like **B3**. A file is a **workbook**, and each page inside it is a **worksheet**. A formula always begins with an equals sign.

tricks.title: Dollar locks what follows
tricks.body: A dollar sign freezes the letter or number right after it. \$A\$1 is frozen both ways. \$A1 freezes the column only. A\$1 freezes the row only.

tricks.title: Count family
tricks.body: COUNT wants numbers only. COUNTA counts anything filled in. COUNTBLANK counts the empty ones. COUNTIF needs a condition.

example.q: A1:A5 holds 10, 20, text, empty, 30. What does COUNT(A1:A5) give?
steps: COUNT counts only numbers.
The numbers are 10, 20 and 30.
Text and empty cells are skipped.

mistakes.wrong: Typing 5+3 in a cell to add.
mistakes.right: Start with an equals sign: =5+3.

mistakes.wrong: Reading cell address B3 as row B, column 3.
mistakes.right: The column letter comes first. B3 is column B, row 3.

mistakes.wrong: Saying Excel has 256 columns in modern versions.
mistakes.right: Excel 2007 and later has 16,384 columns. 256 is the 97-2003 limit.

mistakes.wrong: Using COUNT to count text entries.
mistakes.right: COUNT counts numbers only. COUNTA counts all non-empty cells.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking \$A1 locks the row.
mistakes.right: In \$A1 only the column is locked.

subtopics.notes:
### What Excel does
Excel is a **spreadsheet** program. It stores numbers in a grid and calculates with them. People use it for marks, budgets, bills and charts. A file is a **workbook**. Each page inside it is a **worksheet**.

### Rows, columns and cells
- **Rows** run across and have numbers: 1, 2, 3 and so on.
- **Columns** run down and have letters: A, B, C, and after Z comes AA.
- A **cell** is the box where a row and a column cross. Its name is the **cell address**, such as **B3**. The column letter comes first.
- A **range** is a block of cells, written like **A1:C5**.
- The **active cell** is the one that is selected now. Its address shows in the **Name Box**.
- The **Formula Bar** shows what is inside the active cell.

### Size of a worksheet
| Version | Rows | Columns | Last column |
|---|---|---|---|
| Excel 2007 and later | **1,048,576** | **16,384** | **XFD** |
| Excel 97-2003 | 65,536 | 256 | IV |

The new sheet has 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns. That gives 17,179,869,184 cells in one sheet. A new workbook opens with one sheet in current versions (Sheet1). Older versions opened with three.

> **Tip:** 1,048,576 is 2 to the power 20. 16,384 is 2 to the power 14.

### Formulas start with =
Every formula begins with an **equals sign**. Without it, Excel treats your entry as plain text. For example, `=A1+B1` adds two cells. `=SUM(A1:A5)` adds five cells.

The operators are + (add), - (subtract), * (multiply), / (divide) and ^ (power). Excel calculates in the usual order: brackets, power, multiply and divide, then add and subtract.

> **Rule:** Text typed in a cell leans **left**. Numbers lean **right**.

### Cell references
| Type | Example | Behaviour when copied |
|---|---|---|
| **Relative** | A1 | Changes with the new position |
| **Absolute** | \$A\$1 | Never changes |
| **Mixed** | \$A1 or A\$1 | Only the part without \$ changes |

This matters when you copy a formula down a column or across a row. Press **F4** while editing a formula. It cycles A1, \$A\$1, A\$1 and \$A1.

> **Watch:** A dollar sign locks what comes right after it. In `\$A1` the column is locked. In `A\$1` the row is locked.

### Counting functions
- **COUNT** counts cells that hold numbers.
- **COUNTA** counts all cells that are not empty.
- **COUNTBLANK** counts empty cells.
- **COUNTIF** counts cells that meet one condition.

### Files
Data is saved under a file name in a folder, like any other file. The default extension is **.xlsx** (2007 and later). The older format is **.xls**. A macro file is **.xlsm**. A comma-separated text file is **.csv**. A template is **.xltx**.

patterns.name: Worksheet size and last cell
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the number of rows or columns, or the last column name.
steps: Excel 2007 and later has 1,048,576 rows.
It has 16,384 columns and the last one is XFD.
Excel 97-2003 has 65,536 rows, 256 columns and last column IV.
patterns.why: Both limits are round powers of two, and the exam asks for the version.

example.q: The maximum number of columns in an Excel 2016 worksheet is:
steps: Excel 2016 is newer than 2007.
So the modern limit applies.
The count is 16,384 and it ends at XFD.

patterns.name: Cell address and range
patterns.howToSpot: The question gives an address or range and asks what it means or how many cells it holds.
steps: Read the column letter first, then the row number.
A range uses a colon: start cell to end cell.
Cells in a range = columns wide times rows tall.
patterns.why: The address system is fixed, so the count is simple multiplication.

example.q: How many cells are in the range A1:C5?
steps: Columns A to C make 3 columns.
Rows 1 to 5 make 5 rows.
3 times 5 is 15.

patterns.name: Relative, absolute and mixed references
patterns.howToSpot: The question copies a formula and asks what changes, or asks what a dollar sign does.
steps: Find the dollar signs in the formula.
A locked letter or number never moves when copied.
An unlocked part shifts with the destination.
F4 cycles the four styles.
patterns.why: A copied formula follows how far it moved, unless a dollar sign locks the part.

example.q: A formula =A1 in cell B1 is copied to B2. What does B2 show?
steps: The formula moved one row down.
A relative reference moves too.
A1 becomes A2.

patterns.name: Formula rules and counting functions
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how a formula starts, or which COUNT function fits a situation.
steps: Every formula starts with =.
Use COUNT for numbers and COUNTA for any filled cell.
Use COUNTBLANK for empty cells and COUNTIF for one condition.
patterns.why: The four COUNT functions differ only in what they count.

example.q: Which function counts all non-empty cells in a range?
steps: COUNT would skip text.
COUNTA counts anything that is filled in.

patterns.name: Workbook, worksheet and file types
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the name of the file, the page, or the default extension.
steps: A file is a workbook. A page inside it is a worksheet.
The default extension is .xlsx.
Old format .xls, macro .xlsm, text .csv, template .xltx.
patterns.why: These names are used in every Excel question.

example.q: The default file extension of an Excel 2019 workbook is:
steps: 2019 is after 2007.
The X format applies.

revision: Excel is a spreadsheet program. A file is a workbook and a page is a worksheet.
Cell address = column letter + row number, such as B3. A range looks like A1:C5.
Modern sheet: 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns (last column XFD). Old: 65,536 rows and 256 columns (IV).
Every formula starts with =. Text leans left. Numbers lean right.
Relative A1, absolute \$A\$1, mixed \$A1 or A\$1. F4 cycles them.
COUNT numbers, COUNTA non-empty, COUNTBLANK empty, COUNTIF with a condition.
Files: .xlsx default, .xls old, .xlsm macro, .csv text, .xltx template.

subtopics.title: Functions you must know
subtopics.concept: A **function** is a ready-made formula. It has a name and takes inputs in brackets. Excel groups the common ones into maths, text, logical, lookup and date functions. Learn the exact result of each function, because the exam asks for the output of a given formula.

tricks.title: MOD is the leftover
tricks.body: MOD(a, b) is what is left after a is divided by b. MOD(17,5) is 2, and MOD(10,5) is 0.

example.q: What does =MOD(17,5) return?
steps: 17 divided by 5 gives 3 whole times.
3 times 5 is 15.
17 minus 15 leaves 2.

tricks.title: MID has three inputs
tricks.body: MID(text, start, count). MID("COMPUTER",3,3) starts at the third letter and takes three letters. That gives MPU.

tricks.title: FALSE means exact
tricks.body: The last input of VLOOKUP decides how it matches. FALSE means exact match. TRUE means nearest smaller match.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking INT(7.9) gives 8.
mistakes.right: INT rounds down. INT(7.9) is 7.

mistakes.wrong: Reading MOD(17,5) as 3.
mistakes.right: MOD gives the remainder. That is 2. The 3 is the quotient.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving out the quotes around text in a formula.
mistakes.right: Write text in double quotes, such as "EXCEL".

mistakes.wrong: Using VLOOKUP with TRUE when an exact match is needed.
mistakes.right: Use FALSE for an exact match.

mistakes.wrong: Treating TODAY() as a fixed date.
mistakes.right: TODAY() changes every day. Ctrl+; enters a fixed date.

subtopics.notes:
### How a function looks
A function has a **name** and **arguments** in brackets. For example, `=SUM(A1:A5)`. The arguments are separated by commas. The formula still starts with =.

### Maths functions
| Function | Job | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SUM** | Adds | =SUM(2,3,5) | 10 |
| **AVERAGE** | Mean | =AVERAGE(2,4,6) | 4 |
| **MAX** / **MIN** | Largest / smallest | =MAX(2,9,4) | 9 |
| **ROUND** | Rounds to given digits | =ROUND(3.14159,2) | 3.14 |
| **INT** | Rounds down to whole number | =INT(7.9) | 7 |
| **MOD** | Remainder | =MOD(17,5) | 2 |
| **ABS** | Removes the minus sign | =ABS(-7) | 7 |
| **SQRT** | Square root | =SQRT(9) | 3 |
| **POWER** | Raises to a power | =POWER(2,5) | 32 |

> **Tip:** MOD gives the remainder after division. 17 divided by 5 leaves 2.

### Text functions
| Function | Job | Example | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| **LEFT** | First characters | =LEFT("EXCEL",2) | EX |
| **RIGHT** | Last characters | =RIGHT("EXCEL",2) | EL |
| **MID** | From the middle | =MID("COMPUTER",3,3) | MPU |
| **LEN** | Counts characters | =LEN("EXCEL") | 5 |
| **UPPER** / **LOWER** | Change case | =UPPER("abc") | ABC |
| **PROPER** | Capital first letter of each word | =PROPER("ram kumar") | Ram Kumar |
| **CONCATENATE** | Joins text | =CONCATENATE("A","B") | AB |

**MID** takes three inputs: the text, the start position and the number of characters. Text inside a formula is written in double quotes.

### Logical function IF
`=IF(condition, value if true, value if false)`

For example, `=IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail")` shows Pass when A1 is 40 or more. Otherwise it shows Fail. You can put one IF inside another. That is called a **nested IF**.

> **Rule:** Use AND when all conditions must hold. Use OR when any one is enough.

### Lookup function VLOOKUP
`=VLOOKUP(lookup value, table, column number, FALSE)`

VLOOKUP searches the **first column** of the table. It then returns a value from the column you name. The last input **FALSE** asks for an **exact match**. TRUE (or leaving it out) allows an approximate match. **HLOOKUP** does the same across rows.

### Date functions
- **TODAY()** gives today's date. It has no arguments.
- **NOW()** gives the date and the time.

> **Watch:** Both update every time the sheet recalculates. They are not fixed stamps. Use Ctrl+; for a fixed date.

### Conditional counting and adding
- **COUNTIF(range, condition)** counts cells that meet the test. For example, `=COUNTIF(A1:A10,">40")`.
- **SUMIF(range, condition, sum range)** adds only the cells that meet the test.
- **AVERAGEIF** averages only the matching cells.
- **RANK** gives the position of a number in a list.

patterns.name: Output of a maths function
patterns.howToSpot: A formula with ROUND, INT, MOD, ABS, SQRT or POWER is given, and a result is asked.
steps: Name the function and read its job.
Work with the numbers inside the brackets.
INT cuts down, ROUND goes to the nearest, MOD is the remainder.
patterns.why: Each function has one clear rule, so the result can be worked out by hand.

example.q: What is the result of =POWER(2,5)?
steps: POWER raises the first number to the second.
2 to the power 5 is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 2.
That equals 32.

patterns.name: Output of a text function
patterns.howToSpot: A LEFT, RIGHT, MID, LEN or PROPER formula on a word is given.
steps: Number each letter from 1.
Apply the start position and the count.
Count characters for LEN, spaces included.
patterns.why: Text functions work on positions, so counting letters gives the answer.

example.q: What does =MID("COMPUTER",3,3) return?
steps: Letters are C(1) O(2) M(3) P(4) U(5).
Start at position 3.
Take three letters: M, P and U.

patterns.name: IF and nested IF
patterns.howToSpot: A formula with IF is given and a result is asked for some cell value.
steps: Test the condition with the given cell value.
If it is true, return the second argument.
If it is false, return the third argument.
patterns.why: IF picks one of two answers depending on a test.

example.q: A1 holds 35. What does =IF(A1>=40,"Pass","Fail") show?
steps: The test is false.
The third argument is returned.

patterns.name: VLOOKUP inputs
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks what the fourth input of VLOOKUP does, or which column is searched.
steps: The lookup value is searched in the first column of the table.
The third input is the column number to return.
FALSE gives an exact match. TRUE gives an approximate match.
patterns.why: VLOOKUP always searches the leftmost column, which is why it cannot look left.

example.q: In VLOOKUP, which last argument finds an exact match?
steps: The last argument sets match type.
Exact means no nearest guess.
That is FALSE.

patterns.name: TODAY vs NOW
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which function returns only the date, or the date and time.
steps: TODAY() returns the date only.
NOW() returns the date and time.
Neither takes arguments.
patterns.why: The two names hint at the output, and both refresh on recalculation.

example.q: Which Excel function returns the current date and time?
steps: TODAY gives only the date.
The function with time also is NOW.

patterns.name: Text case and joining
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks which function changes case or joins two pieces of text.
steps: UPPER makes capitals, LOWER makes small letters.
PROPER capitalises the first letter of each word.
CONCATENATE joins the pieces.
patterns.why: Case functions are easy to confuse by name, so match the result.

example.q: Which function converts "ram kumar" to "Ram Kumar"?
steps: The result has a capital at the start of each word.
That is the job of PROPER.

revision: A function has a name and arguments in brackets. Formulas begin with =.
ROUND(3.14159,2) is 3.14. INT(7.9) is 7. MOD(17,5) is 2. ABS(-7) is 7. SQRT(9) is 3. POWER(2,5) is 32.
LEFT and RIGHT take from the ends. MID(text,start,count) takes from the middle. LEN counts characters.
UPPER, LOWER, PROPER change case. CONCATENATE joins text.
IF(condition, true value, false value). Nested IF puts one IF inside another.
VLOOKUP searches the first column. FALSE means exact match. HLOOKUP works across rows.
TODAY() gives the date. NOW() gives date and time.

subtopics.title: Formula errors, charts and data tools
subtopics.concept: Excel shows an **error value** that starts with # when a formula cannot work. Each error has one cause. **Charts** turn numbers into pictures: column, line, pie and scatter. Tools such as filter, PivotTable, Goal Seek and conditional formatting analyse data.

tricks.title: Read the error's name
tricks.body: DIV is division. NAME is a spelling problem. VALUE is a wrong type. REF is a reference that is gone. N/A is not available. NUM is a number problem.

tricks.title: Pie needs one series
tricks.body: A pie chart shows parts of one whole. It uses a single data series. Use line for trends and scatter for two-number links.

example.q: Which chart best shows each state's share of total sales?
steps: Shares of one whole are needed.
That is the pie chart's job.

mistakes.wrong: Calling ##### a formula error.
mistakes.right: It only means the column is too narrow. Widen it.

mistakes.wrong: Blaming #NAME? on a bad number.
mistakes.right: It usually comes from a misspelt function name.

mistakes.wrong: Using a line chart for parts of a whole.
mistakes.right: Use a pie chart for parts of a whole.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing Filter with Sort.
mistakes.right: Sort re-orders rows. Filter hides rows.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking #REF! comes from division by zero.
mistakes.right: Division by zero gives #DIV/0!. #REF! comes from a deleted cell.

subtopics.notes:
### Error values
When Excel cannot finish a formula, it shows an error that starts with #.

| Error | Cause |
|---|---|
| **#DIV/0!** | Division by zero, or by an empty cell |
| **#NAME?** | Excel does not know the name. Usually a misspelt function |
| **#VALUE!** | Wrong type of value, such as adding text to a number |
| **#REF!** | The formula points to a cell that was deleted |
| **#N/A** | A value is not available. Common when a lookup finds no match |
| **#NUM!** | A number problem, such as the square root of a negative number |

> **Watch:** Five hash signs (`#####`) do not mean an error. The column is too narrow to show the number. Widen the column.

### Handling errors
`=IFERROR(value, value if error)` catches any error and shows a replacement. For example, `=IFERROR(A1/B1,0)` shows 0 when B1 is empty or zero.

### Chart types
| Chart | Best for |
|---|---|
| **Column** | Comparing values between items |
| **Bar** | The same, with horizontal bars |
| **Line** | A trend over time |
| **Pie** | Parts of one whole. Uses a single data series |
| **Scatter (XY)** | The link between two numbers |
| **Area** | Change in total over time |

Create a chart from the Insert tab. Select the data first. The shortcut **F11** makes a chart on a new sheet. **Alt+F1** puts a chart on the current sheet.

A chart has a title, axes, a legend, data labels and gridlines. The **X axis** is the category axis. The **Y axis** is the value axis.

> **Tip:** If a question mentions percentages of a total, choose a pie chart.

### Data tools
- **Sort** puts rows in order, from A to Z or from small to large.
- **Filter** hides rows that do not match. The shortcut is **Ctrl+Shift+L**.
- **Conditional formatting** colours cells that meet a rule, such as marks below 40.
- **PivotTable** summarises a large table in a few clicks. It is on the Insert tab.
- **Goal Seek** finds the input that gives a result you want. It is under What-If Analysis on the Data tab.
- **Data Validation** limits what a cell accepts, such as a drop-down list.
- **Freeze Panes** keeps headings in view while you scroll.

> **Example:** Goal Seek answers "What mark do I need in the last test to average 75?"

### Formatting and printing
- **Format Cells** (Ctrl+1) sets number, date, currency and percentage looks.
- **Merge & Center** joins selected cells into one and centres the text.
- **Wrap Text** shows long text on several lines inside one cell.
- **Print Area** and **Page Break Preview** control what prints.
- **Comments** and **Notes** attach remarks to a cell.
- **Sparklines** are tiny charts drawn inside a single cell.

patterns.name: Match the error to its cause
patterns.howToSpot: A situation is described and the error name is asked.
steps: Spot the cause: division, spelling, type, deleted cell, no match, number.
Match it to the error name.
Remember that ##### is a width problem.
patterns.why: Every error has one cause, and the name hints at it.

example.q: Which error appears when a formula divides a number by zero?
steps: Division by zero is the cause.
The error name has DIV in it.

patterns.name: #NAME?, #VALUE! and #REF! compared
patterns.howToSpot: Three look-alike errors are listed and one must be chosen for a cause.
steps: Misspelt function gives #NAME?.
Text used in arithmetic gives #VALUE!.
A deleted cell gives #REF!.
patterns.why: The three are easy to swap, so tie each to its cause.

example.q: =SUMM(A1:A5) is typed by mistake. Which error appears?
steps: SUMM is not a real function.
Excel cannot recognise the name.

patterns.name: Choose the right chart
patterns.howToSpot: A data story is given, and the chart type is asked.
steps: Comparing items points to a column chart.
A trend over time points to a line chart.
Parts of a whole point to a pie chart.
Two-number links point to a scatter chart.
patterns.why: Each chart is built for one kind of story.

example.q: Monthly sales of a shop for 12 months should be shown as a:
steps: The data runs over time.
A trend is needed.
A line chart shows a trend.

patterns.name: Data analysis tools
patterns.howToSpot: The question describes a task and asks for the tool.
steps: Summary of a big table means PivotTable.
Finding a needed input means Goal Seek.
Colour by rule means conditional formatting.
Hiding rows that do not match means Filter.
patterns.why: Each tool answers one type of question.

example.q: Which tool finds the input needed to reach a target result?
steps: The target result is fixed.
The input is unknown.
Goal Seek works backwards.

patterns.name: Chart creation keys and parts
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the key for a chart or the name of a chart part.
steps: F11 makes a chart on a new sheet.
Alt+F1 makes a chart on the same sheet.
X axis holds categories. Y axis holds values.
patterns.why: The shortcuts and axes are short facts asked directly.

example.q: Which key creates a chart on a new chart sheet?
steps: A separate chart sheet is wanted.
The key is F11.

revision: #DIV/0! divide by zero. #NAME? unknown name. #VALUE! wrong type. #REF! deleted cell. #N/A not available. #NUM! number problem.
##### means the column is too narrow. It is not an error.
IFERROR(value, replacement) replaces any error.
Column compares, line shows trend, pie shows parts of a whole, scatter shows a link between two numbers.
F11 makes a chart on a new sheet. Alt+F1 makes an embedded chart.
Filter Ctrl+Shift+L. PivotTable summarises. Goal Seek finds a needed input. Conditional formatting colours cells.

subtopics.title: Excel shortcuts and file facts
subtopics.concept: Excel has its own shortcut keys. **Ctrl+;** enters the date and **Alt+=** adds a sum. **F2** edits a cell and **Ctrl+1** opens Format Cells. Learn them in small groups: entering data, editing, selecting and viewing.

tricks.title: Semicolon for date and time
tricks.body: Ctrl+; enters the date. Add Shift and it enters the time.

example.q: Which shortcut enters the current time in Excel?
steps: Ctrl+; enters the date.
Adding Shift changes it to the time.

tricks.title: Space picks a line
tricks.body: Ctrl+Space picks the column. Shift+Space picks the row. Remember: Ctrl is the taller shape, a column.

tricks.title: D goes down, R goes right
tricks.body: Ctrl+D fills down. Ctrl+R fills right.

mistakes.wrong: Using F11 to insert a worksheet.
mistakes.right: Shift+F11 inserts a worksheet. F11 makes a chart.

mistakes.wrong: Mixing Ctrl+Space and Shift+Space.
mistakes.right: Ctrl+Space selects a column. Shift+Space selects a row.

mistakes.wrong: Using Ctrl+; for time.
mistakes.right: Ctrl+; is date. Ctrl+Shift+; is time.

mistakes.wrong: Using Ctrl+D to copy a cell to the right.
mistakes.right: Ctrl+D fills down. Ctrl+R fills right.

mistakes.wrong: Thinking Ctrl+9 hides columns.
mistakes.right: Ctrl+9 hides rows. Ctrl+0 hides columns.

subtopics.notes:
### Why learn them
Shortcut questions repeat every year. Each key has one fixed job. Learn the groups below.

### Entering data
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+;** | Enters today's date as a fixed value |
| **Ctrl+Shift+;** | Enters the current time |
| **Alt+=** | AutoSum. Adds the numbers next to the cell |
| **Ctrl+E** | Flash Fill. Fills a pattern from an example |
| **Alt+Enter** | Starts a new line inside one cell |
| **Ctrl+Enter** | Fills the selected cells with the same entry |

> **Tip:** Ctrl+; gives a fixed date. TODAY() changes every day.

### Editing and formatting
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **F2** | Edits the active cell |
| **F4** | Cycles reference type. Also repeats the last action |
| **Ctrl+1** | Opens Format Cells |
| **Ctrl+D** | Fill down. Copies the top cell downward |
| **Ctrl+R** | Fill right. Copies the left cell to the right |
| **Ctrl+T** | Makes a table |
| **Ctrl+Shift+L** | Turns Filter on or off |

### Selecting, rows and columns
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Space** | Selects the whole column |
| **Shift+Space** | Selects the whole row |
| **Ctrl+A** | Selects all cells |
| **Ctrl+9** | Hides the selected rows |
| **Ctrl+0** | Hides the selected columns |
| **Ctrl+Home** | Goes to A1 |
| **Ctrl+End** | Goes to the last used cell |

### Sheets and views
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Shift+F11** | Inserts a new worksheet |
| **F11** | Makes a chart on a new sheet |
| **Ctrl+`** | Shows formulas instead of results |
| **Ctrl+Page Down** | Next sheet |
| **Ctrl+Page Up** | Previous sheet |
| **F12** | Save As |

> **Watch:** Shift+F11 inserts a sheet. F11 alone makes a chart. Exams put them side by side.

### Common keys shared with other programs
Ctrl+C copy, Ctrl+X cut, Ctrl+V paste, Ctrl+Z undo, Ctrl+Y redo, Ctrl+S save, Ctrl+P print, Ctrl+F find, Ctrl+H replace, Ctrl+B bold.

> **Note:** Ctrl+; uses the semicolon key, which sits beside the L key.

### Moving around
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Arrow keys** | Move one cell |
| **Tab** | Move one cell right |
| **Enter** | Move one cell down |
| **Ctrl+Arrow** | Jump to the edge of the data block |
| **Ctrl+G** or **F5** | Go To a cell |

### Clipboard and file keys
| Key | Action |
|---|---|
| **Ctrl+Z** | Undo |
| **Ctrl+Y** | Redo |
| **Ctrl+S** | Save |
| **Ctrl+N** | New workbook |
| **Ctrl+O** | Open a workbook |
| **Ctrl+P** | Print |
| **Ctrl+W** | Close the workbook |

> **Tip:** These file keys work the same in Word and PowerPoint. Learn them once and use them in all three programs.

patterns.name: Date, time and AutoSum keys
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the key for date, time or automatic sum.
steps: Ctrl+; enters the date.
Ctrl+Shift+; enters the time.
Alt+= inserts AutoSum.
patterns.why: These three are the most repeated Excel shortcuts.

example.q: The shortcut key for AutoSum in Excel is:
steps: AutoSum needs the Alt key.
It uses the equals sign.

patterns.name: Edit, format and fill keys
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks the key for editing a cell, opening Format Cells or filling.
steps: F2 edits the cell.
Ctrl+1 opens Format Cells.
Ctrl+D fills down. Ctrl+R fills right.
patterns.why: Each key has a memorable link: D for down, R for right.

example.q: Which key puts the active cell into edit mode?
steps: Editing a cell needs the cell to be active.
The function key F2 does this.

patterns.name: Row and column selection and hiding
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks how to select or hide a row or a column.
steps: Ctrl+Space selects a column.
Shift+Space selects a row.
Ctrl+9 hides rows. Ctrl+0 hides columns.
patterns.why: Row and column keys are close, so options swap them.

example.q: Which shortcut selects an entire row in Excel?
steps: A row has a low, flat shape.
The key is Shift+Space.

patterns.name: Sheet, chart and formula-view keys
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for a new sheet, a chart or the formula view.
steps: Shift+F11 inserts a sheet.
F11 makes a chart sheet.
Ctrl+` shows formulas.
patterns.why: F11 with or without Shift does two different jobs.

example.q: Which shortcut inserts a new worksheet?
steps: A chart uses F11 alone.
A sheet adds Shift.

patterns.name: Flash Fill, filter and table keys
patterns.howToSpot: The question asks for the key that fills a pattern, or turns on filter or table.
steps: Ctrl+E starts Flash Fill.
Ctrl+Shift+L toggles filter.
Ctrl+T makes a table.
patterns.why: These newer keys are asked in recent papers.

example.q: Which shortcut turns Filter on or off in Excel?
steps: Filter uses Ctrl and Shift.
The letter is L.

revision: Ctrl+; date. Ctrl+Shift+; time. Alt+= AutoSum. Ctrl+E Flash Fill.
F2 edit cell. F4 cycle references. Ctrl+1 Format Cells.
Ctrl+D fill down. Ctrl+R fill right. Ctrl+T table. Ctrl+Shift+L filter.
Ctrl+Space selects a column. Shift+Space selects a row.
Shift+F11 new sheet. F11 chart sheet. Ctrl+` shows formulas.
Ctrl+9 hides rows. Ctrl+0 hides columns.
Ctrl+Home goes to A1. Ctrl+End goes to the last used cell.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A few cells (may include text or blanks) and "=AVERAGE(...) gives?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Work the function by hand.
SUM and AVERAGE skip text and blank cells.

example.q: A1 = 10, A2 = 20, A3 = "abc" (text), A4 = 30. What does =AVERAGE(A1:A4) return?
example.solution:
Text cell is skipped, so numbers are 10, 20, 30
Sum = 60
Count of numbers = 3
Average = 60 ÷ 3 = **20**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Shortcut for AutoSum" or "shortcut to insert the current date".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Learn: Alt+= AutoSum, Ctrl+; today's date, F2 edit cell.
Ctrl+D is Fill Down, not date.

example.q: The shortcut for AutoSum in MS Excel is:
example.solution:
AutoSum writes the SUM formula for you
It uses the Alt key with the equals key
Ctrl+D is Fill Down, not AutoSum
Answer: **Alt+=**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A cell shows an error code and the reason is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
#DIV/0! = divide by zero. #NAME? = unknown name.
#VALUE! = wrong data type. #REF! = deleted cell. #N/A = not found.

example.q: A cell shows #NAME?. What is the most likely reason?
example.solution:
#NAME? means Excel does not know a word in the formula
Example: =SUIM(A1:A5) has a misspelt function
So the function name is wrong
Answer: **Misspelt function name**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "Which chart best shows a trend over time?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
Line = trend over time. Pie = parts of one whole.
Column or bar = compare categories.

example.q: Which chart best shows the monthly growth of users during a year?
example.solution:
Months in a row = time
Showing change over time needs a line
A pie cannot show time
Answer: **Line chart**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A formula is copied to another cell and the new formula is asked.
pyqPatterns.approach:
References without \$ move with the copy.
\$A\$1 never moves.

example.q: C1 has =A1+B1. It is copied to C3. What does C3 contain?
example.solution:
C3 is 2 rows below C1
Both references have no $, so both move down 2 rows
A1 becomes A3, B1 becomes B3
Answer: **=A3+B3**

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A range with numbers, text and blanks, and "=COUNT(...) gives?"
pyqPatterns.approach:
COUNT counts only numbers.
COUNTA counts all filled cells. COUNTBLANK counts empty cells.

example.q: A1 = 5, A2 = "word", A3 is blank, A4 = 9. What does =COUNT(A1:A4) give?
example.solution:
Numbers are 5 and 9
"word" is text, A3 is empty
COUNT counts only numbers
Answer: **2**

pyqPatterns.pattern: Rows and columns in a sheet
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: "How many rows does an Excel 2007 sheet have?" or "the last column label".
pyqPatterns.approach:
Excel 2007 and later: 1,048,576 rows and 16,384 columns.
The last column is XFD. Old Excel 2003 had 65,536 rows and 256 columns (last IV).

example.q: What is the last column label of an Excel 2016 worksheet?
example.solution:
Excel 2016 has 16,384 columns
Column labels run A to Z, then AA and so on
The 16,384th column is XFD
Answer: **XFD**

solvedExamples.q: Cells A1:A5 contain: 72, Fail, 85, (blank), 90. What does =COUNT(A1:A5) return?
solvedExamples.solution: COUNT counts only numeric cells: 72, 85 and 90 -> 3. The text 'Fail' and the empty cell are ignored (COUNTA would have returned 4).
solvedExamples.shortcut: COUNT = numbers only. Tag each cell N/T/E and count the Ns.

solvedExamples.q: Cell A1 contains 72. The formula =IF(A1>50,"Pass","Fail") displays:
solvedExamples.solution: The condition 72>50 is TRUE, so IF returns its second argument, the text Pass. (If A1 held 40, the third argument Fail would show.)
solvedExamples.shortcut: Evaluate the condition first; return argument 2 on TRUE, argument 3 on FALSE. Plain TRUE/FALSE only appear from a bare comparison like =A1>50.

solvedExamples.q: B1 contains the formula =\$A\$1*2 and is copied to B2. B2 will contain:
solvedExamples.solution: \$A\$1 is fully absolute, so the copied formula is unchanged: =\$A\$1*2. Only relative parts (like A1) would shift row-wise on copying.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Dollar = padlock. \$A\$1 never moves; A1 becomes A2 on a one-row copy.

solvedExamples.q: Which error results from =A1/B1 when B1 is empty?
solvedExamples.solution: An empty cell is treated as zero, so the formula divides by zero and Excel shows #DIV/0!. #VALUE! means a wrong data type, #REF! a deleted reference, #NAME? unknown text.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Blank divisor = zero divisor = #DIV/0!. Don't be fooled into choosing #VALUE! for a blank cell.

solvedExamples.q: How many rows and columns does an Excel 2019 worksheet have?
solvedExamples.solution: Excel 2007 onwards: 2^20 = 10,48,576 rows and 2^14 = 16,384 columns (A to XFD). The 65,536 x 256 grid belongs to Excel 2003 and earlier.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Remember the pair 2^20 x 2^14; the option swapping rows with columns is the deliberate trap.

practice.q: The default file extension of a workbook created in MS Excel 2019 is:
practice.solution: Excel 2007 onwards saves workbooks as .xlsx (Office Open XML). .xls is the 97-2003 format, .xlsm is macro-enabled, .ods is OpenDocument.
practice.shortcut: X = XML = 2007+ across all Office extensions.

practice.q: In Excel, the intersection of a row and a column is called a:
practice.solution: A cell is the single box at a column-row crossing, addressed as ColumnLetter+RowNumber (e.g. B7). A range is a rectangular block of cells.
practice.shortcut: Spreadsheet atom = cell; address = letter + number.

practice.q: Cells A1:A5 contain: 72, Fail, 85, (blank), 90. What does =COUNTA(A1:A5) return?
practice.solution: COUNTA counts every non-empty cell - numbers and text alike: 72, 'Fail', 85, 90 = 4. The blank cell is the only one skipped.
practice.shortcut: COUNTA = Anything non-empty. COUNT would give 3 here.

practice.q: Which function returns the number of characters in a text string?
practice.solution: LEN("text") returns the character count, e.g. LEN("SSCCGL") = 6. There is no LENGTH function in Excel; COUNT works on numbers; CHAR returns the character for an ASCII code.
practice.shortcut: Excel's length function is LEN - no other name exists.

practice.q: Which function displays the current date that updates every time the workbook recalculates?
practice.solution: =TODAY() returns the live current date (updating on recalculation); =NOW() adds the time as well; =DATE() builds a date from given year/month/day; Ctrl+D fills down, it does not insert a date.
practice.shortcut: 'Date only, updating' -> TODAY(); 'date and time' -> NOW(); 'fixed stamp' -> Ctrl+;.

practice.q: VLOOKUP searches for the lookup value in which part of the table array?
practice.solution: VLOOKUP scans the first (leftmost) column of the table vertically and returns a value from the chosen column of the matching row. Searching along the first row is HLOOKUP.
practice.shortcut: V = Vertical = first column; H = Horizontal = first row.

practice.q: The formula =A1/B1 shows #DIV/0!. The most likely reason is:
practice.solution: #DIV/0! means the divisor (B1) is zero or blank. Text in A1 would raise #VALUE!; a narrow column shows #####; a misspelt function shows #NAME?.
practice.shortcut: Divide error -> look at the cell below the slash.

practice.q: A cell displaying ######## (hash marks) indicates:
options: The column is too narrow to show the value
practice.solution: Excel fills the cell with # symbols when the formatted number cannot fit the column width - widen the column. It is a display condition, not an error.
practice.shortcut: Hashes = width, never an error code.

practice.q: Which chart type is best suited to show the trend of monthly sales over a year?
practice.solution: Line charts plot values across a continuous axis - ideal for time-series trends. Pie/doughnut show shares of one whole at a single point; radar compares multiple variables.
practice.shortcut: Trend over time = line, every time.

practice.q: The keyboard shortcut to insert the current date into a cell (as a fixed value) is:
practice.solution: Ctrl+; stamps today's date; Ctrl+Shift+; stamps the time; Ctrl+D fills down from the cell above; Ctrl+T creates a table.
practice.shortcut: Semicolon = stamp. Shift makes it time instead of date.

practice.q: AutoSum is applied with which shortcut?
practice.solution: Alt+= writes =SUM() over the neighbouring numeric range in one stroke. Ctrl+= applies subscript formatting in Word, not AutoSum.
practice.shortcut: Alt with the plus sign = add them up.

practice.q: Which shortcut inserts a brand-new worksheet in the workbook?
practice.solution: Shift+F11 adds a new worksheet. Ctrl+N creates a new workbook (file), and Ctrl+F11 has no default action in modern Excel.
practice.shortcut: New sheet inside the file = Shift+F11; whole new file = Ctrl+N.

practice.q: To find the input value that makes a formula produce a desired result, use:
practice.solution: Goal Seek (What-If Analysis) back-solves one input cell to hit a target output. Pivot Tables summarise data, AutoFilter hides rows, Freeze Panes locks screen areas.
practice.shortcut: You know the answer, want the input -> Goal Seek.

practice.q: The formula =SUM(A1:A5, 10) is entered in B1. A1:A5 contain 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The result is:
practice.solution: SUM adds the range (2+4+6+8+10 = 30) plus the extra argument 10, giving 40.
practice.shortcut: SUM takes every argument: range total first, then any loose numbers.

practice.q: While editing a formula, pressing F4 on the reference A1 changes it to:
practice.solution: F4 cycles the reference through A1 -> \$A\$1 -> A\$1 -> \$A1 -> A1. The first press makes it fully absolute.
practice.shortcut: One tap of F4 = full lock (\$ before both letter and number).

practice.q: How many rows does a worksheet of MS Excel 2007 or later contain?
practice.solution: Excel 2007 onwards has **10,48,576 rows** (1,048,576) and 16,384 columns. 65,536 rows belonged to Excel 2003 and older.

practice.q: The total number of cells in one Excel 2016 worksheet is —
practice.solution: 16,384 columns multiplied by 1,048,576 rows = **17,179,869,184 cells** (about 17.18 billion).

practice.q: The label of the LAST column of an Excel 2007+ worksheet is —
practice.solution: Columns run A to Z, AA to ZZ, ... up to **XFD** (the 16,384th column). IV (256th) was the last column of Excel 2003.
practice.shortcut: 2003 ended at IV; 2007+ ends at XFD.

practice.q: How many rows did a Microsoft Excel 2003 worksheet contain?
practice.solution: Excel 2003 and earlier: **65,536 rows and 256 columns**. The 1,048,576-row grid arrived with Excel 2007.

practice.q: Which cell reference stays COMPLETELY fixed when a formula is copied?
practice.solution: **\$A\$1 is absolute** — dollar signs lock both the column and the row. \$A1 and A\$1 are mixed; only the plain part moves.

practice.q: Cell C1 holds =A1*\$B\$1. It is copied to cell C2 (one row down). C2 will contain —
practice.solution: A1 is relative, so it slides to A2; \$B\$1 is absolute, so it stays. Result: **=A2*\$B\$1**.

practice.q: While editing the formula =A1*2, pressing F4 once changes A1 to —
practice.solution: **F4 adds both dollars first** (A1 to \$A\$1); further presses cycle A\$1, \$A1 and back to A1.

practice.q: Cell D2 holds =B2+\$C\$3. It is copied to E2 (one column right). E2 will contain —
practice.solution: Moving right by one column shifts relative references one letter (B2 to C2); \$C\$3 is locked, so it stays \$C\$3.

practice.q: A file created in MS Excel is called a —
practice.solution: The file = **workbook**; each tab inside it = a worksheet; each box = a cell.

practice.q: The cell at the crossing of column C and row 5 has the address —
practice.solution: Addresses read **column letter first, then row number**: C5.

practice.q: Which screen element shows the address of the active cell?
practice.solution: The **Name Box** (left end of the formula bar) shows where you are; the Formula Bar shows what the cell contains.

practice.q: How many worksheets does a new Excel 2016 workbook contain by default?
practice.solution: One worksheet by default (Excel 2007 onwards; the older default of 3 sheets ended in 2013). More sheets are one click away.

practice.q: When a number is typed in a cell, Excel aligns it to the —
practice.solution: **Numbers right-align, text left-aligns** automatically — a quick test of what Excel thinks your data is.

practice.q: A cell shows a row of #### symbols. This means —
options: The column is too narrow to show the value
practice.solution: ##### is only a **display notice** — widen the column and the number appears. Error values look like #DIV/0!.

practice.q: How many cells does the range A1:B5 contain?
practice.solution: A to B = 2 columns, rows 1 to 5 = 5 rows: 2 x 5 = **10 cells**.
practice.shortcut: cols x rows of the rectangle.

practice.q: Freeze Panes is used to —
options: Protect the file with a password
Stop all editing on the sheet
Keep selected rows or columns visible while scrolling
practice.solution: **Freeze Panes** (View tab) pins headings — the title row stays on screen while long data scrolls under it.

practice.q: What does =SUM(10, 20, 30) return?
practice.solution: =SUM adds its arguments: 10+20+30 = **60**.

practice.q: A1=40, A2=60, A3 blank, A4=80. What does =AVERAGE(A1:A4) return?
practice.solution: AVERAGE ignores the blank cell: (40+60+80)/3 = **60**. Dividing by 4 (giving 45) is the classic trap.
practice.shortcut: Blank cells never join the count.

practice.q: A1=100, A2='exam', A3=50. What does =SUM(A1:A3) return?
practice.solution: SUM skips text cells: 100+50 = **150**. The word 'exam' contributes nothing and raises no error.

practice.q: A1=2, A2=3, A3=4. What does =SUM(A1:A3, 10) return?
practice.solution: SUM adds the range AND the extra argument: 2+3+4+10 = **19**.

practice.q: A1=5, A2='word', A3 blank, A4=9. What does =COUNT(A1:A4) return?
practice.solution: **COUNT counts only numeric cells**: 5 and 9 give **2**. The text and the blank are skipped.

practice.q: A1=5, A2='word', A3 blank, A4=9. What does =COUNTA(A1:A4) return?
practice.solution: **COUNTA counts every non-empty cell** — numbers and text: 5, 'word', 9 give **3**.

practice.q: A1=10, A2='na', A3=30, A4 blank, A5=50, A6 blank. What does =COUNTBLANK(A1:A6) return?
practice.solution: **COUNTBLANK counts empty cells** — A4 and A6 give **2**. (COUNTA here would be 4.)

practice.q: Which function counts ALL non-empty cells, text or number alike?
practice.solution: **COUNTA = count anything filled.** COUNT takes numbers only; COUNTBLANK takes empties; COUNTIF adds a condition.

practice.q: What does =SQRT(144) return?
practice.solution: SQRT is the square root: the square root of 144 is **12**.

practice.q: What does =MOD(23, 5) return?
practice.solution: **MOD gives the remainder**: 23 = 4x5 + 3, so the answer is **3**.

practice.q: What does =ROUND(1234.567, 2) return?
practice.solution: ROUND to 2 decimals: 1234.567 becomes **1234.57** (the third decimal 7 rounds the 6 up).

practice.q: What does =POWER(2, 10) return?
practice.solution: POWER raises the first number to the second: 2 to the power 10 = **1024**.

practice.q: What does =INT(8.9) + =MOD(10, 4) evaluate to?
practice.solution: INT chops the fraction: INT(8.9) = 8. MOD(10, 4) = 2 (remainder). 8 + 2 = **10**.
practice.shortcut: INT = floor for positives; MOD = remainder.

practice.q: What does =LEN('keyboard') return?
practice.solution: **LEN counts the characters**: keyboard has 8 letters, so **8**.

practice.q: What does =LEFT('EXAM', 2) return?
practice.solution: **LEFT takes letters from the start**: the first 2 letters of EXAM are **EX**. RIGHT('EXAM',2) would give AM.

practice.q: What does =MID('computer', 4, 3) return?
practice.solution: **MID(text, start, count)**: from the 4th letter take 3 — c-o-m-**p-u-t**-e-r gives **put**.

practice.q: What does =PROPER('india gate') return?
practice.solution: **PROPER capitalises the first letter of every word.** UPPER would shout INDIA GATE, LOWER goes the other way.

practice.q: What does =CONCATENATE('SS', 'C') return?
practice.solution: **CONCATENATE joins text end to end** with no gap: SS + C = **SSC**. The & sign does the same job.

practice.q: B2 holds 38. What does =IF(B2>=40, 'Pass', 'Fail') display?
practice.solution: 38 is not greater than or equal to 40, so the condition is FALSE and the third value, **Fail**, is shown.

practice.q: VLOOKUP searches for the lookup value in which part of the table?
practice.solution: **V = vertical search down the FIRST column**; the column-number argument only decides what is returned after the match is found.
practice.shortcut: VLOOKUP always enters from the left door.

practice.q: A1:C3 holds: 101 Pen 10 / 102 Pencil 5 / 103 Eraser 3. What does =VLOOKUP(102, A1:C3, 3, FALSE) return?
practice.solution: It finds 102 in the first column and returns the 3rd column value of that row: the price **5**.

practice.q: In VLOOKUP, the FALSE (or 0) argument asks for —
options: An exact match of the lookup value
practice.solution: FALSE = **exact match**; TRUE (or omitted) allows the nearest smaller value in sorted data. Exact is the safe choice with codes.

practice.q: B1 is empty. What will =A1/B1 display?
practice.solution: An empty cell counts as zero, so the formula divides by zero: **#DIV/0!**.

practice.q: You type =SUIM(A1:A5). What does Excel show?
practice.solution: SUIM is not a function Excel knows — unrecognisable text gives **#NAME?**.

practice.q: A1 contains the text 'exam'. What does =A1+5 show?
practice.solution: Adding a number to text is the wrong data type: **#VALUE!**.

practice.q: A formula refers to cells in column D, and those cells are deleted. The formula shows —
practice.solution: The reference is gone, so Excel reports **#REF!** (invalid reference).

practice.q: A VLOOKUP searches for code 999 which does not exist in the table. The result is —
practice.solution: **#N/A means 'not available'** — the lookup value was not found in the first column.

practice.q: Which chart type best shows the trend of temperature month by month?
practice.solution: **Line charts draw trends across time** — the eye follows the rise and fall directly.

practice.q: To show how the annual budget is split among departments, use a —
practice.solution: A **pie chart shows shares of one whole** — each slice is one department's percentage of the budget.

practice.q: To compare the marks of five students in one test, the clearest chart is —
practice.solution: **Column (or bar) charts compare values between categories** — five students, five columns, tallest wins.

practice.q: To study the relationship between height and weight of 50 people, use a —
practice.solution: **Scatter plots two number variables** as points — clusters and trends reveal the relationship.
practice.shortcut: Two numbers = dots on a grid.

practice.q: You want to see only the rows where the city is Pune, without deleting anything. Use —
practice.solution: **Filter hides** the non-matching rows; the data stays safe and comes back when the filter is cleared.

practice.q: Which feature summarises lakhs of sales rows into a compact category-wise table?
practice.solution: A **PivotTable** drags fields into rows, columns and values to summarise huge data within seconds.

practice.q: Failing marks (below 35) should automatically turn red. Use —
practice.solution: **Conditional formatting** paints cells when a rule (here <35) is true — the colour updates itself as values change.

practice.q: Which tool arranges selected rows from A to Z or smallest to largest?
practice.solution: **Sort reorders** data ascending or descending; Filter only hides; both keep every row intact.

practice.q: In a chart, the small key that tells which colour belongs to which series is the —
practice.solution: The **legend is the chart's key** — e.g. blue = 2024, orange = 2025.

practice.q: The exact value printed on top of each bar is called a —
practice.solution: **Data labels print the number on each bar or slice**, so the reader need not measure against the axis.

practice.q: In a normal column chart, category names (like city names) usually appear on the —
practice.solution: Column charts put **categories on the x-axis and values on the y-axis**; bar charts swap them.

practice.q: The shortcut to insert today's date as a fixed value in a cell is —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+; stamps today's date** (fixed text). Ctrl+D fills down — the planted trap.

practice.q: Which shortcut runs AutoSum on the selected cells?
practice.solution: **Alt+= is AutoSum** — it writes =SUM() over the neighbouring numbers in one stroke.

practice.q: Which key edits the content of the active cell directly?
practice.solution: **F2 puts the cursor inside the cell** for editing. F4 toggles references, F12 is Save As.

practice.q: Pressing Ctrl+D with a cell selected in Excel will —
options: Copy the content of the cell above into it (fill down)
practice.solution: **Ctrl+D = fill down** — the date stamp is Ctrl+;. Mixing these two is the most repeated Excel trap.

practice.q: The default file extension of an Excel 2007 or later workbook is —
practice.solution: **.xlsx** is the Office Open XML default (X = XML); .xls is the 97-2003 file.

practice.q: A workbook that contains macros should be saved as —
practice.solution: **m = macro**: .xlsm keeps macros; .xlsx silently drops them.

practice.q: A .csv file stores data as —
options: Plain text values separated by commas
practice.solution: **CSV = Comma Separated Values** — one sheet, no formatting, opens in any program.

practice.q: Which extension belongs to the Excel 97-2003 format?
practice.solution: The X-less **.xls** is the pre-2007 format; every X variant is 2007 or later.

practice.q: Which key combination jumps to cell A1?
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Home goes to A1**; Ctrl+End jumps to the last used cell.

practice.q: Ctrl+End takes the cursor to —
options: The end of the current row
The last used cell of the data
practice.solution: **Ctrl+End lands on the bottom-right of the USED area** — not necessarily the grid's absolute corner.
practice.shortcut: End of your data, not of Excel.

practice.q: To move to the next worksheet of a workbook, press —
practice.solution: **Ctrl+Page Down / Page Up** walk through the sheet tabs; Ctrl+arrows move within the data.

practice.q: Which shortcut inserts a new worksheet into the open workbook?
practice.solution: **Shift+F11 adds a worksheet**. Ctrl+N opens a whole new workbook; F11 alone makes a chart sheet.

practice.q: The fastest way to rename a worksheet is to —
options: Double-click its tab, type the new name
practice.solution: A **double-click on the sheet tab** opens the rename box (right-click, Rename also works).

practice.q: Which key opens the Save As dialog in Excel?
practice.solution: **F12 = Save As** (in every Office program); Ctrl+S saves in place.
